claim: A teacher, department or school cannot authorise use of a language for its community; the authority (a Nation's council, language authority, Elders' committee, or a school board acting with them) decides, in writing.
source: policy, following CARE (Carroll et al. 2020) and the field-linguist review

claim: Every item needs two layers of consent (speaker or family; the authority), and consent given for documentation does not cover machine learning.
source: policy; Tanzer et al. 2024 shows renewed permission was sought for machine-learning use

claim: For a speaker who has passed on, the family normally decides.
source: common practice reported in the field-linguist review

claim: In Canada, TCPS 2 (2022) chapter 9, Article 9.1, requires community engagement where research is likely to affect an Indigenous community's welfare.
source: TCPS 2 (2022), chapter 9 (checked by the field-linguist review)

claim: forge keeps each model's list of source files, so a model can be retrained without withdrawn files.
source: forge run identity, which includes the training files' hashes

claim: The agent starts no training until the authority's decisions are written down; forge does not yet enforce this (build list A1).
source: agent rule; forge status as of 2026-10-14

claim: Learners never see unreviewed machine output; they see a bank of outputs a speaker has checked.
source: policy; interviewees worried learners would learn the language wrongly (Mager et al. 2023)

claim: Health information is not a use for this kind of translator; use human translation and a qualified interpreter.
source: policy; interviewee views split on health (Mager et al. 2023); even commercial engines left harmful errors in high-resource languages (Khoong et al. 2019)

claim: Classic text collections often hold sacred or ceremonial narratives recorded under consent that did not foresee machine learning; the best-known classic Plains Cree collection is, by its title, sacred stories dictated in 1925 and freely readable online.
source: Bloomfield 1930, Sacred Stories of the Sweet Grass Cree (National Museum of Canada Bulletin 60); field-linguist review

claim: Nothing goes in until a reviewer the authority appoints classes it as open, community-only or excluded; anything not yet classed is excluded; the agent never fetches language text on its own.
source: policy (agent rule); forge enforcement missing (build list A2, A6)

claim: Plan 24 to 30 hours per 1,000 pairs of about 6 English words at a professional translator's pace (40 to 50 at 10 words).
source: derived from Maillard et al. 2023 (200 to 250 words an hour)

claim: One speaker giving 2 hours a week adds about 70 to 80 six-word pairs a week (67 to 83); 6,400 pairs would take 77 to 96 weeks.
When an elder dictates to a scribe, total person-hours per pair double.
On Klingon, about 1 short everyday sentence in 5 was exactly right at 6,400 pairs (18.7 to 19.6%) and about 1 in 4 at 12,800 (23.2 to 23.7%).
No published system for a polysynthetic language, and no forge run on a real language, has been shown to reach 8 in 10 sentences meaning-right.
source: absence in the reviewed literature (AmericasNLP 2021/2023, Inuktitut, Mapudungun) and forge's runs

claim: With 100 judged sentences, 80 right gives a 95% interval of about 71% to 87%.
forge offers two default bars: 'useful draft' (at least 50% meaning-right) and 'working' (80% meaning-right, judged on the Wilson lower edge); the community sets its own.
forge keeps the test set on the computer, sends no file to a rented machine without a typed yes for that exact file, and shows every score with its uncertainty.
source: forge README; forge remote lane; forge scoring (95% CIs)

claim: MADLAD-400 3B lists Klingon (a <2tlh> tag) but with zero pairs scored chrF++ 8.6, 0 of 1,000 exactly right, and copied the English back in 33% of outputs.
No open model forge can fine-tune knows Klingon: NLLB-200 has no Klingon code, MADLAD-400 lists it but cannot translate it untrained, and ByT5's pretraining data (mC4) has no Klingon label.
Microsoft Translator, a closed commercial service, lists Klingon (Latin and pIqaD).
source: a third-party language list; not verified against Microsoft's own pages

claim: Tatoeba's Klingon is in OPUS and the Tatoeba-Challenge, so models trained on those may have seen it.
source: OPUS API listing; Tatoeba-Challenge README v2023-09-26

claim: Klingon is agglutinative, not polysynthetic: verb prefixes for subject and object, suffixes in fixed ordered slots, no noun incorporation; its grammar was designed to be regular.
source: Klingon's published affix grammar as used in forge's analysis; field-linguist review

claim: Tatoeba sentences are licensed CC BY 2.0 FR (attribution; no share-alike or non-commercial limit).
source: Tatoeba terms of use and downloads page; per-sentence licence field

claim: forge's Klingon split: 21,898-pair training pool by the main author; test-main 1,000 sentences by the same author (5.8 English words on average); test-other 1,001 by other authors; dev 501; rows sharing an English or Klingon sentence kept together.
30% of test-main and 29% of test-other sentences have a near-twin in the training pool.

Tatoeba's downloads contain direct translation links only; in a 300-sentence sample, 21.0% (about plus or minus 5 points) of Klingon sentences with any English translation reached English only through a third language and are dropped by direct-only selection.
source: Tatoeba downloads page and PairsExporter source; sample via the Tatoeba search API, 2026-10-14

claim: Pairs reached through a third language are a legitimate but noisier source, kept in their own labelled lane and never in dev or test.
source: policy; chained links are the likeliest to be loose (Tatoeba contributor profile)

claim: OPUS lists 16,911 English-Klingon pairs; forge counted about 21,898 from the main author; the two are not reconciled.
No speaker review has certified the Tatoeba Klingon.
source: Tatoeba contributor profile; no certification found

claim: forge recorded two exact-match figures differing by up to about 2.4 points (analysis 18.7-19.6% and 23.7%; scorer lane 16.8-17.7% and 21.3%); the analysis figure is reported throughout.
source: forge Klingon calibration records and curve analysis

claim: ByT5-small training on a 24 GB M4 Pro Mac: 15 min (400 pairs), 40 min (1,600), 84 min (3,200), 4.1-4.2 h (6,400, memory-pressured), 2.4-2.6 h (12,800, 10 passes).
The training seed alone moved Klingon chrF++ 5.2 points at 1,600 pairs and 0.7 at 6,400; no size between was run twice; forge's analysis says verdicts can flip by chance below about 5,000 pairs.
source: forge measurement and analysis on Klingon (Tatoeba)

claim: Below about 5,000 pairs, run three seeds and require a round's gain to exceed the seed band.
source: policy from forge's Klingon seed results and the MT review (M3, M7)

claim: At 12,800 Klingon pairs: sentences of 1-4 English words 31-34% exactly right, 5-7 words 23-24%, 8 or more 7%; short sentences came out right 4 to 5 times as often.
source: forge measurement on Klingon (Tatoeba); ratio derived

claim: Klingon exactly-right gains per doubling: +7 to +9, then +9 to +10, then about +4 points (1,600 to 12,800 pairs).

On one fixed set of 309 test-main sentences (in vocabulary at 6,400 pairs), exactly right rose from 37.5-38.2% (6,400, two seeds) to 42.4-42.7% (12,800, two seeds) and 43.4% with back-translation (one seed); more random pairs still improve the translator, slowly.
The earlier claim that in-vocabulary accuracy was flat from 6,400 to 12,800 pairs compared different sentence sets at each size and is withdrawn.
source: MT review M1; forge fixed-subset re-analysis

claim: forge's analysis uses two in-vocabulary definitions: every word seen (shares 35% then 47%, accuracy 34-36%) and every English word plus every reference word seen (shares 31% then 43%, accuracy 36-38%), each on different sentences at each size.

forge's Klingon word splitter was built from the published affix grammar and stems learned from Tatoeba's Klingon text; an agent found no stem wrong in 120 random words, 19 of 20 common words right, and 4.8% of words with a near-equal second reading.
source: forge Klingon curve analysis (agent check, not a speaker)

claim: In-lexicon Klingon sentences (every stem seen) were exactly right 25-26% at 6,400 pairs and 28-29% at 12,800 (different sets at each size); the invented language got 94% with in-lexicon shares within 5 points of Klingon's.
source: forge measurement on Klingon (Tatoeba) and its invented test language

claim: Of Klingon one-word misses at 12,800 pairs: 43-44% a known stem with a wrong ending, 51-52% another known stem, 5% a stem never in training.
source: forge measurement on Klingon (Tatoeba), heuristic word splitter

claim: Klingon decoding at 12,800 pairs: greedy 56.5 chrF++ / 23.2% in 22 s per 1,000 sentences; beam 4 56.9 / 23.2% in 42 s; MBR 58.1 / 22.8%; word-list gate 20.8-21.8%; best of 8 by the reference 67.1 / 38.9%; reverse-model chooser 23.3% to 23.6% (test-other 24.8% to 25.1%).
MBR decoding with a chrF utility optimises the yardstick: on Klingon it raised chrF++ by 1.6 while exactly right fell from 23.2% to 22.8%.
source: forge measurement on Klingon (Tatoeba); MT review M2

claim: Back-translating 10,196 Klingon sentences at 12,800 pairs: test-main +1.6 chrF++ and +1.7 points exactly right; test-other +0.9 and +1.1; one run, one seed; training took about twice as long (4.4 h against 2.5 h).
By forge's reading, the back-translation lane bought about a third of what 6,400 more real pairs bought between 6,400 and 12,800 pairs (one run, one test set).
ByT5-small's full recipe used about 16 GB of a 24 GB Mac's GPU memory, ran out of memory at a 12 GB cap (step 1,037), and held 19 GB uncapped.
NLLB-600M full fine-tuning ran out of memory at forge's earlier 16 GB cap at batch 8 (step 800 of 8,000); NLLB-1.3B with LoRA ran out at step 72.
Pausing training while a person used the shared Mac cost 1.1 to 1.5 hours per overnight job.
The Klingon memory and time figures come from short, Latin-script, nearly ASCII sentences; byte-level models' memory and time grow with byte length.
source: forge Klingon data; MT review M10

claim: An agent read 60 one-word Klingon misses and judged 29 likely acceptable in meaning (95% interval 36% to 61%), which would put meaning-right near 34-40% at 12,800 pairs; no speaker has rated Klingon outputs.
source: forge Klingon analysis (agent reading); interval derived

claim: A commissioned Klingon test set (at least 300 new English sentences, at least two qualified speakers, CC0 or CC BY, sealed until the first headline score, plus a blind meaning review of 100 outputs) is the cleanest independent test.
paq'batlh: The Klingon Epic, 2nd edition (2022), is published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and suits only an out-of-domain evaluation stress test, scored internally, never trained on.
source: Zenodo record 19849412; forge Klingon data-sources research

claim: forge's invented test language reached 79% meaning-right at 6,400 pairs (77-81% over three seeds) and 86% at 12,800, with the same recipe and computer.
source: forge measurement on its invented test language

claim: Median width of the 95% interval on a chrF++ difference on the invented language: about 11 points at 23 sentences, 7-8 at 50, 5.3 at 100, 3.8 at 200; a real language should give wider intervals.
source: forge measurement on 500 held-out invented-language outputs (60 draws per size); direction caveat from MT review M4

claim: AmericasNLP 2023: one native speaker per language rated 50 sampled outputs for three languages on a 1-5 meaning scale (4 = general meaning conveyed, some details may be missing); top ratings were rare; most Otomí outputs got the lowest.
AmericasNLP 2021: mean human adequacy about 2 of 5 for Shipibo-Konibo and Otomí, with no visible correlation between chrF and the human scores.
source: Mager et al. 2021 §5 (checked by the MT review)

claim: English to Inuktitut, in domain: segment-level Kendall tau with fluent experts 0.293 for chrF against -0.004 for sentence BLEU.
A single second-language annotator (50 sentences per direction) saw no consistent preference between Mapudungun systems despite a 3-point chrF++ gap.
AmericasNLP 2023 best chrF ranged 15.3 (Otomí) to 40.4 (Guarani) on training sizes from 357 (Chatino) to 125,008 (Quechua) pairs plus extra data.
source: Ebrahimi et al. 2023 Table 1 and results

claim: Ten AmericasNLP test sets are translated natural-language-inference sentences; Chatino's is legal text, scored 39.97 chrF on 357 pairs.
source: Ebrahimi et al. 2023 (checked by the MT review)

claim: WMT20 English to Inuktitut: chrF 37.9, BLEU 15.8 with about 1.3 million parliamentary pairs plus news.
Nunavut Hansard: 20.3 BLEU into Inuktitut against 35.0 out of it, partly a BLEU effect.
source: Joanis et al. 2020; caveat from MT review m5

claim: Mapudungun with NLLB, 55,452 pairs: into Mapudungun 39.9-42.9 chrF++ (600M to 3.3B) with no gain from morphology-aware tokenisation; out of Mapudungun 34.9-45.8 (600M: 34.9 standard, 43.2 with vocabulary-constrained Morfessor).

Bilingual from scratch, 1,000 / 3,000 / 6,000 professionally translated pairs gave average chrF++ 12.6 / 19.9 / 22.9, English into the target (13.2 is the table average at 1,000 because of missing cells).
In a multilingual setting with pre-existing data, the 6,000-pair seed beat back-translation (up to 2 million sentences per language) in all but one case.

Multilingual models with related languages scored about 10-16 chrF++ above bilingual models on the same 6,000-pair seed (e.g. Venetian 33.5 to 49.5; Sicilian 29.6 to 41.8), confounded with extra pre-existing data.
source: Maillard et al. 2023 Tables 2 and 5 (checked by the MT review)

claim: AmericasNLP winners trained multilingually: 2021 Helsinki multilingual model; 2023 Sheffield multi-stage multilingual NLLB; 2025 the organisers' joint NLLB-1.3B beat per-language NLLB-3.3B fine-tunes for 12 of 13 languages per track.
source: Mager et al. 2021; Ebrahimi et al. 2023; de Gibert et al. 2025

claim: Quechua lifted Asháninka (521 pairs) from 1.3 to 5.9 BLEU; adding Asháninka to Quechua plus Finnish lowered Quechua from 22.6 to 17.0.
Kalaallisut data slightly lowered chrF into Inuktitut (51.9 to 50.6 / 51.3).
Same-family multilingual Bible training collapsed for Cree and Navajo but helped Inuit-Aleut languages by 4.2 BLEU on average.
Training with a similar high-resource language beat plain adaptation by 1.7 BLEU on average.
Related-language and dialect data enters as a tagged lane per language, with dev and test on the target only and terms per lane, kept only if dev improves.
source: policy from MT review B3 and the evidence above

claim: The Quechua system that scored 23.4 BLEU in domain scored 1.4 and 0.6 out of domain.
source: Chen & Fazio 2021 Table 3 (checked by the MT review)

claim: Cherokee: 15.8 BLEU in domain against 6.5 out of domain.
Training only on religious text lost 59-96% of the news score.
A religious-corpus benchmark overstated quality on everyday text.
Hand-revising a 7,281-pair Nheengatu set to 6,848 pairs gave a markedly better translator.
Copied untranslated rows at 5% of the data cut BLEU from 27.2 to 17.6 (German-English).
A mined English-Quechua corpus was 47% near-duplicates, with 21.8% of the rest in the wrong language.
With a strong reverse model, back-translation recovered 67-83% of the gain of the same amount of real pairs; with a weak reverse model, beam outputs beat sampled ones.
The original back-translation recipe mixed real and synthetic 1:1; tagging the synthetic side matches or beats noising.
source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch 2016; Caswell et al. 2019

claim: In one high-resource study the best back-translation ratio was 2 synthetic per real, by about 0.007 BLEU; in another, 1:1 gave +0.8 BLEU and 3:1 +0.6; with tags, larger amounts are used.
source: Poncelas et al. 2018; Fadaee et al. 2017; Maillard et al. 2023

claim: Back-translation: tag it, start at one synthetic per real pair, and tune the ratio on dev.
source: policy from MT review M6 and the evidence above

claim: In-domain monolingual text gave +5.4 BLEU from back-translation against +0.3 out of domain; Bribri gained +1.0 BLEU only in domain; filtered back-translation gave +0.8 chrF++ for NLLB-600M.
source: Hoang et al. 2018; Feldman & Coto-Solano 2020; Gu et al. 2023

claim: A 1,146-entry dictionary added about 1-2 BLEU on top of monolingual pretraining (Kannada-English); a curated lexicon added +4.9 chrF in a 200-language model, parallel data did more, and both together most.
source: Koneru et al. 2022; Jones et al. 2023

claim: Gemini 1.5 Flash, English to Kalamang chrF++: nothing 11.0; explanations only 22.6; example sentences only 26.6; wordlist 29.1; whole book 34.4.
Over 16 languages, adding a grammar to a wordlist and retrieved sentences lowered English-to-X chrF++ from 30.3 to 26.7 (GPT-4-turbo).
The ranking 'texts, then dictionary, then grammar prose' holds for training an NMT model; for LLM prompting the wordlist beat the example sentences.
source: Aycock et al. 2025; MT review m13

claim: Grammar prose cannot train an NMT model; its example sentences can, once cleared.
source: how NMT training works (parallel text only)

claim: Across 30 languages with paradigms of 12 to over 700 forms (a Cree among them), adding forms the model got wrong helped most and adding forms it already got right could lower accuracy (inflection, not translation).
25,056 forms of 792 lemmas in 15 languages were elicited remotely with bracketed English context.
A consultant's translation is evidence to be checked, not proof.
Having speakers check FST-generated forms in natural carrier sentences is usually faster than producing every paradigm cell.
source: fieldwork practice reported in the field-linguist review; not measured here

claim: An FST rejects missing stems, other dialects' forms, loanwords, names, new coinages and other spellings, so a rejected word is not necessarily wrong.
source: how finite-state analysers work; field-linguist review M10

claim: forge's validity floor applies only to generated (synthetic) rows, not to speakers' own sentences.
source: forge FAILURE_TAXONOMY 3.4 (target-validity gate on synthetic lanes)

claim: Ojibwe verbs: mean chrF 0.82 (0 to 1 scale) on a self-built 214-verb test; 83.5% of the first 1,500 generated English-to-Plains-Cree phrases fully well-formed.
A rule-based system won the 2025 Nahuatl word-formation task at 17.5% where most systems scored 0 to 4%.
One Plains Cree analyser holds 21,232 stems (2022 count).
Analyser segmentation lost to plain subwords: Inuktitut 23.3 against 27.7 BLEU; Guarani 7.1 against 10.5.
Unsupervised morphology-aware segmentation beat tuned subwords in 5 of 8 directions at 7,442-14,208 pairs, by up to +4.16 chrF (Spanish to Rarámuri), and lost on Nahuatl.
Rule-generated Q'eqchi' data gave 42.0 BLEU on its own synthetic test and 0.59 on real text; swapping and re-inflecting words gave +0.4 to over +3 BLEU in 11 of 14 non-polysynthetic pairs.
source: Chulzhanov et al. 2026; Ibn Alam et al. 2024

claim: Into English (30,000-pair base plus 20,000 selected), quality-estimate selection beat random by about 2.0, 1.7 and 0.3 BLEU (Swahili, Kinyarwanda, Spanish); round-trip-likelihood selection did worse than random; gains are about one standard deviation.
Pure n-gram selection fell 0.4-2.6 BLEU below random in 17 of 18 Kannada-English cells.
Crowd workers took 11.98 s per word for highlighted phrases against 32.92 s for whole sentences (MTurk wall-clock including idle time, Urdu to English).
Transcription takes at least 10:1 (monologue) or 15:1 (conversation) hours per hour of audio for a skilled fluent transcriber, 15:1 to 30:1 with checking, about 50:1 with translation.
ByT5 scored higher chrF++ than mT5 at every size, by up to about 10 points at 400 pairs (large models), on high-resource languages ByT5 had already seen; COMET found the two competitive.
source: Edman et al. 2024 (checked by the MT review)

claim: ByT5 trained 4-5 times and translated 5-6 times slower than mT5.
Into 16 African languages (half absent from M2M-100's pretraining), average BLEU / chrF: M2M-100 418M 15.4 / 41.1; mBART-50 13.2 / 37.5; ByT5-base 10.9 / 31.9 (M2M-100 ahead by 9.2 chrF).
source: Adelani et al. 2022 Table 3 (checked by the MT review)

claim: Out of the 16 African languages, M2M-100 scored 17.7 against 14.1 BLEU for ByT5; continued pretraining added 0.6-0.9 BLEU for ByT5.
The default base comparison from about 1,000 pairs is three-way: ByT5-small, M2M-100 418M or mBART-50, and NLLB-600M with full fine-tuning where its licence allows.

NLLB-600M on Limbum: zero-shot chrF++ 12.5; from-scratch Transformer 14.5; fine-tuned on about 7,000-8,800 pairs 46.7-47.3 on an in-domain test; new tag initialised from related languages; learning rate 5e-5.
source: Limbum study 2026 (anonymised preprint; reports give 7,070 and 8,837 pairs)

claim: Plains Cree is not among NLLB-200's languages.

LoRA evidence is mixed: rank-256 LoRA on NLLB-3.3B matched full fine-tuning for Spanish-Quechua (36.40 against 36.39) and lost 0.9 for Spanish-Guarani (35.24 against 36.13); on NLLB-600M over 13 pairs, full 25.12, OFT 25.06, LoRA 25.27 on dev; on mBART-50 LoRA 18.6 against 30.3 full.
source: Garcia Gilabert et al. 2024; Stackhouse & Debenedetto 2026 (abstract-level); Su et al. 2024

claim: forge's nllb-600m preset is LoRA rank 16, with no translation evidence found for that rank; forge has no full-fine-tuning NLLB preset yet.
source: forge presets; absence in the reviewed literature

claim: Never rank forge's LoRA rank-16 NLLB preset against a fully fine-tuned ByT5.
Into Bhili, fine-tuned NLLB-600M scored chrF++ 35.2 against 21.2 for Llama-3-8B and 19.4 for Qwen3-8B.
Into Kalamang at about 1,200 pairs, NLLB-1.3B scored chrF++ 34.2 against 13.0 for Llama-3.1-8B with LoRA.
With 500,000 Spanish-X examples over 11 languages, Llama-3-8B averaged 17.2 chrF++ (one pass) and 20.9 (five passes); the best system compared against, a multilingual NMT model, scored 26.7.
source: Iyer et al. 2024 (checked by the MT review)

claim: Three LLMs prompted Spanish to Wixarika scored under 3 BLEU and 21 chrF, with output unrelated to the source.
LLM editing of NLLB drafts: into Spanish a median of +0.6 chrF++ over 13 languages, worst -11.7 (Chatino); into Awajún 16.67 against 35.09 for the draft.
source: Hus, Krasner & Anastasopoulos 2025; median derived from the paper's table

claim: Gemini 1.5 Pro with about 250,000 tokens of Kalamang material scored 59.0 chrF English to Kalamang against 57.0 for a human learner.
source: Gemini Team 2024 (MTOB section; one language, a small test)

claim: At community data sizes, never let a general-purpose LLM write the language.
source: policy from Singh et al. 2025, Aycock et al. 2025, Iyer et al. 2024, Gagnier & Kirubakaran 2026, Hus, Krasner & Anastasopoulos 2025

claim: At 5,000 pairs from scratch, a tuned Transformer gained +6.0 BLEU over the default; a tuned RNN went from 0.0 to 16.6 BLEU.
Checkpoint averaging gave +1.69 chrF++ for NLLB-600M on small sets.
Full fine-tuning with AdamW holds 16 bytes per weight before activations; Adafactor about half; gradient recomputation costs about 30% more time.
source: Hugging Face documentation; Shazeer & Stern 2018; Chen et al. 2016

claim: Training state (AdamW / Adafactor): ByT5-small 4.8 / 2.4 GB; M2M-100 418M 6.7 / 3.3; NLLB-600M 9.8 / 4.9; NLLB-1.3B 20.8 / 10.4; MADLAD-400 3B about 47 / 24.
source: derived: parameters x 16 or about 8 bytes

claim: Apple chips trained 3-4 times slower than similarly priced NVIDIA cards in one study.
T5-family models can overflow in fp16; use fp32 or bf16 (bf16 on a Mac needs macOS 14).
source: Hugging Face documentation and forum reports

claim: ByT5, mT5 and MADLAD-400 weights are Apache-2.0; M2M-100 and mBART-50 are MIT; NLLB-200 is CC BY-NC 4.0, so a fine-tuned NLLB is best treated as non-commercial adapted material.
source: model cards; CC BY-NC 4.0 legal code (our reading; not legal advice)

claim: forge's own licence is PolyForm Noncommercial.
Sequence-level knowledge distillation trains a small student on a strong teacher's translations; no measurement exists for a polysynthetic language.
source: Kim & Rush 2016; absence in the reviewed literature

claim: Professional translators for 39 low-resource languages averaged 200-250 words an hour, on Wikipedia-domain sentences, with source or target words unstated, paid USD 25.80 an hour on average.
Hours per 1,000 pairs at 6 / 10 English words: forge's early figure 17 / 22; professional 24-30 / 40-50; crowd 55 / 91; post-editing good output 5 / 8; weak output 27 / 45.
source: derived from Maillard et al. 2023, Bloodgood & Callison-Burch 2010, Meetei et al. 2020

claim: Post-editing took 2.93 s per output word on good output and 16.14 s on weak output; typing in a non-Latin script took 4.8 s a word against 2.6 s in Roman script.
No published rate exists for fluent community speakers translating short everyday sentences.

Weekly yield at professional pace: 2 h gives 67-83 (6-word) or 40-50 (10-word) pairs; 9 h 300-375 or 180-225; 20 h 667-833 or 400-500; weeks to 6,400 pairs 77-96 / 128-160, 17-21 / 28-36, 8-10 / 13-16.

Speaker hours to reach each Klingon stage at professional pace (6-word / 10-word): 1,600 pairs 38-48 / 64-80; 6,400 154-192 / 256-320; 12,800 307-384 / 512-640; dev 100 plus test 200 single-translated about 7-15.
source: derived from Maillard et al. 2023's rate

claim: Fluent speakers are often over-worked and over-burdened and few may be literate enough to transcribe; one listening study recruited 6 participants for Kanien'kéha where an English one recruited 30 in 30 minutes.

Elders often work for free; long sessions need rest and medication breaks and room for grief; speakers want copies returned to them and to community archives; some want co-use copyright inherited by descendants.
chrF can look good on bad output: Nigerian Pidgin scored chrF about 60 while humans judged 20% of outputs nonsense or the wrong language.

COMET-22 agreed with humans less than chrF++ on 6 of 13 African language pairs (e.g. Luo 0.062 against 0.279); COMET scored a Chinese-script output for a Russian reference (0.536) above an empty line (0.316).
source: Wang et al. 2024; Zouhar et al. 2024

claim: Averaged over many language pairs, a 1.0-point chrF difference agreed with humans on which system is better 70% of the time and 3.05 points 90%; this is system-level on large test sets, mostly high-resource.
source: Kocmi et al. 2024 Table 2 (checked by the MT review)

claim: XSTS agreement (Fleiss kappa) averaged 0.55, the mean of 0.43 (into English) and 0.67 (out of English), ranging 0.12-0.99 by language, with trained professional raters; XSTS 3 means mostly equivalent, no significant conflicts in meaning.
source: Licht et al. 2022 Table 3 and Fig. 1 (checked by the MT review)

claim: Three raters on 100 items is underpowered for small effects.
Communities said a few widely respected and community-engaged language speakers would be practically sufficient to assess the pedagogical value of speech models.
source: Pine et al. 2022 §4.1 (an analogy from speech synthesis)

claim: The only published translator-productivity thresholds are for English to Spanish: sentence BLEU above 45, TER below 30.
In one reproduction, test items whose answers leaked scored up to 83.8 BLEU against 30.9-39.2 for clean ones.
Random splits give optimistic estimates; translationese references distort evaluation.
source: Søgaard et al. 2021; Graham, Haddow & Koehn 2020

claim: Test sets are built from new, never-published sentences, because public text may be inside a base model's pretraining crawl, and are author- or speaker-disjoint from training.

The round verdict keeps a new model only if the paired-bootstrap 95% interval on the dev chrF++ difference excludes zero, the gain exceeds the three-seed band below about 5,000 pairs, exactly-right and in-lexicon accuracy on fixed subsets do not fall, and one primary arm is preregistered with Holm correction for the rest.

claim: Two judges combine as 'right only if both say right', with each judge's rate, disagreements and Cohen's kappa reported.

claim: At the sizes an earlier draft gave, power was 0.60 (n = 70, true 90%), 0.51 (n = 250, true 85%) and 0.25 (n = 100, true 85%).

claim: CARE principles: collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, ethics.

forge today has: split, verify-split, leak-audit (near-twin removal), the dev fence, prereg and ledger, scores with intervals and compare-runs, draft-newer and speaker-verdict, wishlist and analyze, grow-dev, the model presets, memory fitting, the remote lane, export, serve and choose, and private-text withholding.

forge does not yet have: Step-0 and inventory enforcement, author-disjoint splits, a seed band, fixed-subset in-vocabulary scores, FST error typing, a tokenizer audit, M2M-100 / mBART-50 / full-NLLB presets, related-language lanes, a back-translation command, distillation, a laptop-CPU speed check, or a recorded release decision.
